hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? what’s the most precious thing anyone has ever given you?
options: then this story might surprise you. listen.
then you already know the secret of this one. listen.
that’s a lovely problem. keep a few in mind. listen.

steps.line: Long ago, a great king named Artaban owned a pearl so fine that people said no one could put a price on it.
He sent it to Rabbi Yehuda, the great sage of the Jewish people, with a message: “Send me something just as precious.”

steps.q: What do you think the rabbi sends back?
o: A small scroll of holy words
A blessing, in the rabbi’s own hand
steps.why: A mezuzah: a tiny handwritten scroll, worth almost nothing in coins.

steps.line: The rabbi sent back a mezuzah: a tiny scroll, written by hand, made to be fixed to the doorpost of a home.
Inside are words from the Torah, beginning: “Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one.” The same passage says, write them on your doorposts.
The king was offended. “I sent you something priceless, and you send me something worth a coin?”

steps.q: A real mezuzah scroll can’t be printed. Who has to make it?
o: A trained scribe, by hand, on parchment
Any rabbi, with a blessing said over it
The family, on the day they move in
steps.why: A sofer writes it with a quill and special ink, letter by letter. One missing or broken letter makes it unfit.

steps.line: The rabbi answered: “You sent me something I must guard. I sent you something that guards you, even while you sleep.”

steps.q: The Talmud says the scroll in a home’s mezuzah should be checked. How often?
o: Never, once it’s been put up
steps.why: Twice in seven years, since ink fades and parchment cracks. Something that guards you needs looking after too.

steps.line: Today, many Jewish homes have a mezuzah on the right doorpost as you walk in, often slanted. Many people touch it as they pass.
steps.label: today

o: So rainwater runs off the parchment
So the top points toward Jerusalem
Two teachers disagreed; it’s a bit of both
steps.why: Rashi said hang it upright; his grandson Rabbeinu Tam said lay it flat. Many Ashkenazi Jews slant it, honoring both. Many Sephardi Jews hang it upright.

say: here’s what i love. the rabbi’s gift was worth almost nothing in coins, and it was the one that kept watch.
in jewish tradition the mezuzah isn’t a lucky charm. the great teacher maimonides said so himself. it’s the words, and what they remind you of, every time you cross the door.

steps.q: The king measured gifts by price. By the rabbi’s measure, which gift was worth more?
o: The pearl: no one could price it
The scroll: it looks after its keeper
steps.why: The scroll. One treasure you lock away. The other you live with, every time you walk through your door.

today.say: today, as you leave home, rest your fingers on the doorframe for one second, the way people touch a mezuzah, and carry one good word out with you.
options: that little touch is the whole idea. take the words with you.
that works too. your door will still be there tomorrow.

sources: Jerusalem Talmud, Peah 1:1 (Artaban sends Rabbi a priceless gem or pearl; Rabbi sends a mezuzah; ‘you sent me something I must guard, I sent you something that guards you while you sleep’)
Proverbs 6:22 (cited by Rabbi in the story: ‘when you lie down it shall watch over you’)
Deuteronomy 6:4–9 (the Shema; write them on the doorposts of your house, 6:9)
Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam on the mezuzah’s position (Tosafot, Menachot 33a); Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De’ah 289:6, with the Rema (the slant)
Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Mezuzah 5:4 (not an amulet)
Babylonian Talmud, Menachot 33b; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De’ah 289:2 (the right side, as you enter)
check: Artaban’s gift: the Hebrew margalit is often rendered ‘pearl’, sometimes ‘precious stone’; the lesson says pearl
The king’s complaint paraphrased as ‘worth a coin’ (the Yerushalmi names a small coin, a follar); Rabbi’s reply paraphrased
Artaban described only as ‘a great king’ (usually identified as a Parthian king, Artabanus); parallel in Genesis Rabbah 35:3 to confirm
